summary: An Our World in Data article by Hannah Ritchie and Max Roser, first published June 2020 and revised January 2024, examining how much CO₂ the world emits and which countries emit the most. It covers global emissions over time, regional and per capita differences, cumulative historical contributions, and how emissions are measured and estimated, including the Canada 1900 example and the China overestimation case. Boilerplate such as navigation, citation and licensing text is ignored.
one_line: Our World in Data article on global CO₂ emissions over time, by region, per capita, cumulative historical totals, and measurement methods.
key_facts: The article was first published in June 2020 and last revised in January 2024 by Hannah Ritchie and Max Roser.
In 1950 the world emitted 6 billion tonnes of CO₂, and by 1990 this had almost quadrupled to more than 20 billion tonnes.
The world now emits over 35 billion tonnes of CO₂ each year.
In 1900, more than 90% of emissions were produced in Europe or the US.
The US and Europe now account for less than one-third of emissions.
The world's largest per capita CO₂ emitters are major oil-producing countries, most in the Middle East, including Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, and Kuwait.
In many of the poorest Sub-Saharan African countries such as Chad, Niger, and the Central African Republic, the average footprint is around 0.1 tonnes per year.
Asia accounts for around half of global emissions, and China emits more than one-quarter of global emissions.
North America is the second largest regional emitter at one-fourth of global emissions, and Africa and South America each account for 3-4% of global emissions.
The UK was the world's largest emitter until 1888, when it was overtaken by the US.
The United States has emitted around 400 billion tonnes of CO₂ since 1751, almost one-quarter of historical emissions, more than 1.5 times China's contribution.
The UK is now responsible for less than 1% of global emissions.
China overestimated its annual emissions in 2013 by using global average emission factors, a finding from Liu et al. (2015), resulting in a 10% overestimation of global emissions.
More typically, uncertainty in global CO₂ emissions ranges between 2-5%.
Historical fossil fuel CO₂ emissions can be reconstructed back to 1751 based on energy statistics.
Since 1751 the world has emitted over 1.5 trillion tonnes of CO₂.
